## Two studies to set beside our five {.smaller}

::: {.small}
The disagreement among our five analysts follows a pattern that was described first, and at far greater scale, in two studies on which the rest of this part rests.
:::

:::: {.fragment}
::: {.small}
**Silberzahn and colleagues (2018)** – the red-card study from earlier, in which twenty-nine teams analysed one dataset to answer one question. Twenty of the twenty-nine intervals excluded 1, and nine did not.
:::

```{r}
#| label: silberzahn-strip
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 1.5
# The same 29 published estimates as the Part 1 forest, flattened onto one row
# as a reminder. Hollow rings so the cluster
# between 1.2 and 1.5 stays countable where filled dots would merge.
ggplot2::ggplot(silberzahn29, ggplot2::aes(or, y = 1, colour = significant)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "longdash", colour = grey_mid) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(shape = 21, size = 5.5, stroke = 1.3, fill = NA) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = ncl_blue, `FALSE` = d_red),
                      breaks = c("TRUE", "FALSE"), name = NULL,
                      labels = c("significant", "not significant")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3)) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.8, 3.05), ylim = c(0.94, 1.06)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "odds ratio, 29 teams", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(13) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "right", legend.key.spacing.y = grid::unit(2, "pt"),
        legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 10, colour = "grey25"),
        axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "grey92"))
```
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
**Auspurg and Brüderl (2021)** went back through all twenty-nine of those analyses and asked a question that the original had not: what was each team actually trying to measure?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The first establishes that careful people disagree, and the second explains **why**.
:::

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne; @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial
:::

::: notes
Before we go further into our own case study, I set two studies beside it, one of which you have already met. [advance] In the red-card study of Silberzahn and colleagues, twenty-nine teams worked on one dataset and one question, and twenty intervals excluded one while nine did not; the chart flattens all twenty-nine onto a single line, so that you can take in their spread. That study establishes that careful people disagree. [advance] The second study is new, and the rest of this part depends on it. Auspurg and Brüderl, in 2021, went back through all twenty-nine analyses and asked what each team had actually been trying to measure. [advance] The first study shows the disagreement, and the second explains it.
:::

## Four estimands in the red-card study {#they-were-not-answering-the-same-question}

:::: {.none}
<br>
Auspurg & Brüderl re-read the 29 analyses and found **four** different estimands:

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
descriptive association, discrimination *net of mediators*, variance-maximising, exploratory
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
The dispersion came largely from a multiverse of **questions**, rather than from a multiverse of analyses.
:::
::::

::: {.src}
@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial
:::

::: notes
Auspurg and Brüderl found that the twenty-nine teams had been answering four different questions. [advance] Some estimated the plain descriptive association, some discrimination proper, the effect net of everything that legitimately explains red cards, some built models tuned to explain variance, and some were openly exploring. With four questions in play, the answers were bound to differ. [advance] This reading changes the debate about the crisis considerably, because much of what looks like instability in analysis is unstated disagreement about what is being estimated.
:::


## Red-card estimates with and without a fixed estimand {#fix-the-estimand-and-the-spread-collapses}

```{r}
#| label: redcard-contrast
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.2
# Dispersion contrast. TOP ROW IS REAL: the 29 published estimates, the same
# file that the Part 1 forest reads. BOTTOM ROW IS A SKETCH: Auspurg & Brüderl
# give the median (1.28) and SD (0.06) of their 486-model multiverse but not
# the 486 values, so these are evenly spaced quantiles of a normal on exactly
# those two numbers – deterministic, and reproducing the published summary by
# construction rather than by a lucky seed.
ab <- qnorm(seq(0.5, 485.5, by = 1) / 486, mean = 1.28, sd = 0.06)
contrast <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(grp = "29 teams,\nquestion left open", or = silberzahn29$or),
  tibble::tibble(grp = "486 models,\nestimand fixed", or = ab)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(grp = factor(grp, levels = c("486 models,\nestimand fixed",
                                             "29 teams,\nquestion left open")))

ggplot2::ggplot(contrast, ggplot2::aes(or, grp, colour = grp)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "longdash", colour = grey_mid) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(shape = 21, fill = NA, size = 4.6, stroke = 1.1, alpha = 0.75) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 3.0, y = 2.42, label = "SD 0.45", hjust = 1,
           colour = d_red, fontface = "bold", size = 4.6) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 3.0, y = 1.42, label = "SD 0.06", hjust = 1,
           colour = ncl_blue, fontface = "bold", size = 4.6) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(ncl_blue, d_red)) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3)) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.8, 3.05), ylim = c(0.7, 2.6)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "odds ratio", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(14) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "grey92"))
```

::: {.small}
- Fix the question, derive the model space from a DAG, and run **all 486** justifiable models: the SD falls from **0.45 to 0.06**
- The 0.45 in the top row comes mostly from **two analyses**, the outliers beside a tight cluster
:::

::: {.src}
@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial. Top row: the 29 published estimates. Bottom row: drawn to their reported median (1.28) and SD (0.06) – the 486 values are not published.
:::

::: notes
Auspurg and Brüderl then fixed one estimand, discrimination properly defined, used a causal graph to derive every specification consistent with it, four hundred and eighty-six in all, and ran them all. The standard deviation falls from point four five among the twenty-nine teams to point zero six with the question fixed. The top row shows the twenty-nine published estimates, and only the bottom row is drawn to the reported median and standard deviation, because the four hundred and eighty-six values were never published. Most of the spread in the top row comes from two outliers beside a tight cluster. The workshop follows the procedure of their study: a precise question, the assumptions drawn out explicitly, then a whole multiverse rather than one path, and then the analysis of sensitivity.
:::


## Under-specified research questions {#the-crisis-has-a-crisis-of-its-own .smaller}

:::: {.none}
Auspurg and Brüderl put the question in their title: *has the credibility of the social sciences been credibly destroyed?*

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
If the twenty-nine teams answered **four different questions**, most of their disagreement is not evidence that analysis is unreliable.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
It is evidence that **the question was under-specified** – an ordinary, fixable defect.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Read this way, the many-analyst literature is a **diagnosis of vague research questions** rather than a verdict on social science.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
This reading is more optimistic, and also more demanding, because it places the problem with whoever writes the question.
:::
::::

::: {.src}
@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial
:::

::: notes
Auspurg and Brüderl put the consequence of their diagnosis into their title, asking whether the credibility of the social sciences has been credibly destroyed. [advance] If the twenty-nine teams were in fact answering four different questions, most of their disagreement is not evidence that data analysis is unreliable. [advance] It is evidence that the question handed to them was under-specified, an ordinary and fixable defect of research design. [advance] Read in this way, the literature on many analysts becomes a diagnosis of vague research questions rather than a verdict on the field. [advance] I find this a considerably more optimistic reading, and also a more demanding one, because it takes the problem away from statistics, where one could hope that a better estimator would help, and places it with whoever writes the question, which in the tasks ahead means you.
:::
